Uterine Cancer
NRBS 4210
Sophie Hieronymi, Michelle Iczkovits, Abigael Kamar, Jassica 
Kaur, Angelena (Lena) Parker, Safra Pernier, 
Sara Spiro, Shavorn Thompson

Uterine Cancer Risk Factors and Health Promotion
Risk Factors
© SUNY Downstate Health Sciences University 2021 – Privileged & Confidential 2
Health Promotion
“Most uterine cancers are endometrioid (i.e., originating in the lining of the 
uterus). Type 1, which accounts for about 80% of cases, is estrogen dependent. 
It is usually low grade with a favorable prognosis. Type 2, which occurs in about 
20% of cases, is high-grade, not estrogen-dependent, and usually serous cell or 
clear cell. Older and Black females are at higher risk for type 2.”
● Screening is important for anyone with a uterus, 
regardless of presentation or gender identity
● All individuals with a uterus should have annual 
checkups that include a gynecologic exam
● Weight loss and patient education about  
unopposed estrogen therapy can be preventative 
measures

Clinical Manifestations
● Abnormal uterine bleeding is the most common symptom of EC
● Pyometra (uterine infection) and vaginal discharge may accompany the bleeding
● End-stage manifestations: Pelvic pain, ascites, unexplained weight loss, fatigue, bowel/ bladder changes, and signs of 
metastasis (lungs, liver, bone)
© SUNY Downstate Health Sciences University 2021 – Privileged & Confidential 3
Prevention and Early Detection
● Abnormal bleeding is the most common early indicator 
● Endometrial hyperplasia is a precursor to endometrial cancer and can be detected by biopsy
● Patients taking tamoxifen should be monitored for endometrial cancer

Diagnostic Tests
● Female patients are encouraged to have checkups and gynecologic examinations annually.
○ Female patients with irregular bleeding or postmenopausal women with bleeding may require additional examinations 
including endometrial aspiration/biopsy to rule out hyperplasia and transvaginal ultrasound to measure endometrial 
thickness. 
● Diagnostic tests to confirm the presence of uterine cancer require a biopsy or aspiration for tissue pathology. 
● Nursing Implications
○ Pre-Biopsy
 Ensure informed consent is completed.
 Review lab results and ensure availability of donor blood if needed.
○ Monitor vital signs and patient positioning (lithotomy) during the procedure.
○ Post-Biopsy
 Monitor for signs of bleeding.
 Educate to avoid placing anything in the vagina for 72 hours to prevent infection.
© SUNY Downstate Health Sciences University 2021 – Privileged & Confidential 4

Medical Management
Surgery 
● Total hysterectomy + bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy 
(BSO) 
● ± lymph-node assessment
Radiation
● Vaginal brachytherapy and/or external-beam radiation 
therapy (EBRT)
● Used for selected intermediate/high-risk disease
● Frequently administered as adjuvant therapy following 
surgery
Systemic Therapy
● First-line chemotherapy: Carboplatin + paclitaxel
● Immunotherapy and targeted biological agents
● Treatment selection is increasingly guided by specific 
tumor biomarker status 
Hormonal Therapy
● Progestins used for hormone-receptor-positive disease
● Considered in selected low-grade or recurrent cases
● Viable medical option when fertility preservation is desired
© SUNY Downstate Health Sciences University 2021 – Privileged & Confidential 5
CLINICAL TAKEAWAY
• Early-stage: Surgery ± Radiation  |  • High-risk / Advanced: Multimodal Therapy  |  • Recurrent / Metastatic: Systemic therapy guided by tumor biology

Nursing Responsibilities
Chemotherapy: Carboplatin + Paclitaxel
● Monitor CBC for neutropenia, anemia, and thrombocytopenia
● Assess for peripheral neuropathy with paclitaxel
● Monitor for hypersensitivity/infusion reactions
● Administer prescribed antiemetics and assess nausea/vomiting
Hormonal Therapy: Progestins
● Monitor for thromboembolism (leg swelling, pain, SOB)
● Assess for weight gain, edema, and abnormal bleeding
● Reinforce medication adherence
Immunotherapy/Targeted Therapy
● Monitor for treatment-specific adverse effects
● Report new rash, diarrhea, respiratory symptoms, or signs of organ 
inflammation
● Review labs and assess for toxicity before treatment
Key Nursing Priorities
Monitor for infection and bleeding related to bone marrow 
suppression.
Assess for treatment toxicity such as nausea, fatigue, neuropathy, 
and infusion reactions.
Educate the patient about medication side effects and when to 
contact the healthcare provider.
6

Patient and Family Education
● Warning signs 
○ Bleeding after menopause
○ Abnormal vaginal bleeding/ discharge
○ Pelvic pain
○ Unintentional weight loss
● Risk factors
○ Taking estrogen without progesterone
○ Diabetes
○ Nulliparity/ infertility 
○ Early menarche/ late menopause
● After treatment
○ Report vaginal/ rectal bleeding
○ New lumps
○ Leg swelling
○ Unintentional weight loss
○ Connect with support/social work as needed 
© SUNY Downstate Health Sciences University 2021 – Privileged & Confidential 7

Discharge Planning: Activity and Treatment
Rest & General Mobility
● Expect fatigue and weakness; pace activities and rest throughout 
the day.
● Move around gradually as tolerated; ask family/friends for 
assistance with meals and chores.
Specific Activity Restrictions
● Stairs: Go slowly, rest every few steps, and ensure someone is 
present initially.
● Lifting: Strictly adhere to prescribed weight limits; avoid heavy 
objects until cleared.
● Driving: Do not drive while taking prescription narcotic pain 
medications or before pain-free.
● Exercise & Work: Consult healthcare provider before resuming 
work duties or exercise regimens.
8
CLINICAL TAKEAWAY
• Rest as needed, advance movement gradually, adhere to lifting limits & med safety •  Neutropenia: Check temperature daily  & call for fever ≥100.4°F (38°C)
Infection Risk & Monitoring
● Chemotherapy and radiation destroy neutrophils (and all WBC), 
heightening infection risk. WBC are normally low 7-12 days after 
each chemotherapy dose. 
● Keep appointments to monitor levels via blood work
● Fever may be the primary or only warning sign of infection
Critical Precautions and Actions
● Maintain a working digital thermometer and log daily temp.
● Contact oncology team immediately for fever ≥100.4°F (38°C); fever 
is a medical emergency
● Receive annual flu shots; avoid live vaccines; ensure household 
members are vaccinated
● Educate family on strict hand hygiene and infection prevention 
protocols.

Home Care
9© SUNY Downstate Health Sciences University – Privileged & Confidential
Rest & Activity
● Expect fatigue and rest as needed; ask family/friends to assist with 
chores.
● Resume movement gradually; take stairs slowly with support.
● Adhere strictly to lifting limits; do not drive while on prescription pain 
meds.
● Perform hospital-taught coughing & deep breathing exercises.
Nutrition & Bowel Health
● Prevent constipation: eat high-fiber foods, drink plentiful fluids, and 
request stool softeners if needed.
Medications & Hygiene
● Take only prescribed medications and pain management strictly as 
directed.
● Shower only when approved; keep surgical site clean & dry.
● Wash hands often with soap and water, especially before eating, 
after using the bathroom and after being outside.
● Avoid tub baths, swimming, and vaginal insertion until cleared.
Incision & Surgical Site
● "Urgent Medical symptoms" warning signs patients should look out 
for after uterine surgery that may require prompt medical evaluation
● Check incision daily for redness, swelling, warmth, foul drainage, or 
opening.
● Bright red / foul vaginal bleeding, severe abdominal pain, bloating, 
or persistent vomiting.
● Urinary burning/difficulty, chest pain, shortness of breath, or arm/leg 
swelling and redness.

NCLEX Question 1
Case Study
Mrs. U is a 66-year-old white female who came to the medical clinic 
at an independent living community for older adults; she is 
concerned about recent post-menopausal bleeding. The nurse is 
gathering additional information before the patient is seen by the 
provider. 
● Vitals: BP 130/85; HR 72; temp. 98.1 F; RR 16; O2 sat. 99%
● BMI: 31 kg/m2
● OB-Gyn History:
○ Menarche age 10
○ G3P3 
○ Early menopause (age 45)
○ Multiple recent sexual partners
❖ Multiple sexual partners
❖ Menarche age 10 
❖ BMI
❖ Race 
❖ Obstetric history 
❖ Age
© SUNY Downstate Health Sciences University 2021 – Privileged & Confidential
The nurse knows that Mrs. U is at increased risk of uterine 
cancer due to her  _______ , ______, and _______. 
10
CORRECT: Menarche - early onset of 
menstruation increases risk of uterine 
cancer; BMI - women with obesity are 
three times more likely to develop uterine 
cancer; Age - women > 50 years, with 
average age of diagnosis 63.
INCORRECT: Multiple sexual 
partners increases risk for cervical, not 
uterine cancer; Race is not a risk factor; 
OB hx - Nulliparity, not multiparity, 
increases risk.

NCLEX Question 2 - SATA
A. Mrs. U will likely die because Type 1 uterine cancer has a 
poorer prognosis than Type 2.
B. Type 1 endometrial cancer is estrogen dependent.
C. There are several surgical treatment options depending on the 
cancer staging.
D. Radiation treatment is rarely used for uterine cancer.
E. Mrs. U will have regular blood tests to monitor for cancer 
antigen 125.
Answers and Rationale
A. INCORRECT. Type 1, which accounts for 80% of uterine cancers, has a 
favorable prognosis and is usually low-grade.
B. CORRECT. This type of cancer is estrogen dependent, which is why age 
at menarche and menopause are risk factors.
C. CORRECT. Medical management may involve surgical resection only, or 
a partial or total hysterectomy may be necessary.
D. INCORRECT. Radiation is part of many treatment plans, along with 
surgery and chemotherapy. It is infrequently used for ovarian cancer not 
uterine cancer.
E. CORRECT. Rising levels of CA-125 in the blood is one indicator that 
cancer has recurred or metastasized so labs are vital.
